name: Daria Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team of eight chat agents at a big telecom company, the ones who sort out broadband faults when your internet drops. I start at eight with the overnight queue, check which faults are area-wide, then spend the day coaching agents, jumping on the angry chats and doing the rota. I use AI every day, I've built little prompt templates so my agents can draft replies faster. I'm also on the staff council, which my boss finds slightly annoying.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out the most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The rota and the angry customers both, but in different ways. The rota is a puzzle, the customers are just tiring, especially on Mondays when everyone's router died over the weekend. I'm honestly not the most organised manager yet. My partner Lou says I bring the queue home in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: good, now we can stop pretending the chatbot will fix everything and actually staff the queue properly. I'd say it in the staff council too. Online I'd share it with a slightly smug comment, I'll admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the tools. But I'd also know the routine stuff, like password resets and "is there an outage in my area", would still go to a bot. That's maybe a fifth of what my agents do, and that matters for them even if it doesn't touch me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep improving my templates and teach the whole team to use them, so the time saved goes to the hard chats, not to cutting heads. I'd push in the council for an agreement that saved time doesn't mean fewer staff. Then I'd get on with the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly fine for me, worried for the newer agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would that fifth of the work hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Jordan and Bea, who mostly take the easy chats. If the chatbot takes the easy broadband chats, the two newest agents on my team lose the only chats they're confident with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And for you personally, how safe does your job feel in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty fine. Good pay, savings, and every other telecom and bank in the city wants team leads. I'm the least worried person in this picture, honestly.

I'd raise it at the **staff council** too.
think: She'd be a bit **disappointed**, because she likes the tools.
Routine chats, about **a fifth** of the work, would still move to a bot.
do: Teach the whole team her **prompt templates** for drafting replies.
Push the council for an agreement that saved time means **no cuts**.
feel: **Uneasy** for her newer agents, mostly fine for herself.
S0.quote: If the chatbot takes the easy broadband chats, the two newest agents on my team lose the only chats they're confident with.
fieldNote: She's secure herself but **worried for juniors** whose easy chats go to bots.
She wants time saved by AI spent on **hard chats**, not cuts.
Her enthusiasm for AI sits alongside a **union-style** instinct to protect staff.

steps.text: Teach all eight agents her prompt templates for fault replies
Push the staff council for a no-cuts agreement on saved time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a deal, written down, on what happens to people when the software takes their tasks. Answering customers is literally on the list, so my team is first in line. I'd be posting about it, and I'd want the company held to whatever it promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think chat support halves in two or three years, and the people left handle the weird cases. I could be one of the people who runs the AI side, because I already use it every day. I'm more worried about my agents than about me, but I'm also not senior, so I might just be one of the cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the project that sets up the support bot, because I'd rather design it than have it done to us. I'd fight in the council for retraining money, so agents can move into fault engineering or sales. And I'd take a course on how these systems are built, probably online, in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like before a big exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be leading the project that shrinks your own team. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me up. I'd be building the chatbot that takes half my team's jobs, and I'd tell myself it's better me than someone who doesn't care about the team. I'm not sure that's entirely true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair deal for your agents look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone gets a real offer: a course, a new role or a fair payout, not a letter on a Friday. And I'd want my agents to hear it from me first, not in a group email.

fieldNote: She'd **build the tool** that cuts her own team, and she admits that sits badly with her.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the support chatbot project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments have to act like it's a crisis, because it is. Basic income, free retraining, a pause on mass layoffs while people adjust. I'd be out on the street for that, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 my job is gone and so is the job of setting up the bots, because AGI can do that too. My comfort is that I'm 27, I've got savings and my partner's work isn't the same as mine. But all my clever plans from the slower picture are useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more of my salary into savings straight away, and stop the trip to Japan Lou and I were planning. I'd look at moving to a public body, maybe the city council's digital services, because they'll keep humans in the loop longer by law. And I'd join a proper union, not just the staff council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly frightened, for the first time in this conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is all screen work. Does the three-year robot gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, it doesn't help much. Lou is a graphic designer, and that's thinking work too. My partner and I both work on screens, so the three years before the robots come are three years for plumbers, not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest, I'd say we'd be fine for a year and then we'd see. My dad drives a bus. I've never thought his job would outlast mine, and now I'm not so sure.

say: I'd call it a **crisis** and demand basic income and free retraining.
I'd be **on the street**, not just posting.
think: Her job and the job of **building bots** are both gone by 2028.
Being **27 with savings** is her only real comfort.

steps.text: Cancel the Japan trip and save the money instead

March for a basic income and free retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so start now: retraining funds, a shorter week, and companies sharing what they save. I'd be loud in the council and online. I'd also say to friends that they need to start learning these tools tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I can ride this for a few years, since I'm good with the tools. I'd probably get two or three years running AI support, then need something else. The thing I'd want to land in is the part where people decide what the AI is for, not the part where it does the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the chatbot project in the first year and get that on my CV. Then I'd do a part-time master's in public policy, about technology and work, paid from savings. By year four I'd want a job advising councils or unions on how to bring these systems in fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful too. It's the first one where I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the master's doesn't lead anywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't go hungry, which is a privilege, and I know it. Five years is long enough for someone like me with savings to retrain, and far too short for my agents who live payday to payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the agents are worse off. What does that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push even harder for them, I hope. A savings cushion makes me brave, and I'd want to use that bravery for the people who don't have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want a national plan for every job the AI touches. I'd say that at work and at every family dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this is the one where I feel I can win. I'm 27, I like the tools, and in ten years I can build a whole second career. I'd be 37 with real experience in how AI changes work, and that would be worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the chatbot project, then move into a policy or strategy role within three years. On the side I'd help small charities set up AI support, maybe for a fee, to learn and earn. And Lou and I would probably buy a flat in year two, because we'd know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. Mostly excited, which I feel guilty saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel guilty. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, some days. Because I know I'm in a better spot than most. Ten years with savings and AI skills feels like a head start, and I feel guilty that my head start is someone else's ten-year countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the charity work be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a couple of chats a week, for about the same money as a nice holiday. It's not about the money, it's about being useful outside the company.

I'd ask for a **national plan** for every job AI touches.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because all my plans depend on having a few years to move, and that one doesn't give me any. All my plans are about staying one step ahead of the AI, and AGI by 2028 is the picture where there's no step left to take. What would help is basic income and free retraining, and a law that companies talk to staff before they cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the guilt part. I like these tools, I use them every day, and I'm also scared of what they do to people like my agents. I don't think I'm unusual in feeling both. Nobody asks about that.

headlineQuote: All my plans are about staying one step ahead of the AI, and AGI by 2028 is the picture where there's no step left to take.
portrait: Daria is **27** and leads eight broadband chat agents at a large telecom company.
She uses **AI every day**, builds prompt templates for her team, and sits on the staff council.
She has strong **savings** and lives with her partner Lou, a graphic designer.
In slower pictures she'd **build the chatbot** and then move into policy work on AI and jobs.
She feels both **excited and guilty**, knowing her head start is her agents' countdown.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves no time for the moves her plans depend on.
whatWouldHelp: **Basic income** and free retraining while people move.
A law that companies **consult staff** before cutting.
